..
Issued at 125 PM CST Thu Nov 5 2026

Recent GOES-19 water vapor imagery depicts an upper-level 
trough propagating southeastward through the Great Lakes region.
Per surface observations from regional airports, a cold front 
is also racing southward across the Great Lakes today tied to a 
parent low pressure system centered in central Quebec. Expansive
low-level stratus blankets the Great Lakes regions on either 
side of the front within the cyclonic shear axis of the trough, 
which is leading to a muted diurnal temperature response 
(current readings locally are in the lower 50s). Meanwhile, a 
secondary upper-level wave anchored by seasonably cool low- to 
mid-level temperatures (around -5C at 850mb per a 00Z sounding 
from Churchill, Manitoba yesterday evening) is evident diving 
southward over Lake Superior at press time. Increasing low- 
level isentropic ascent ahead of the cold front and secondary 
upper-level trough is maintaining spotty showers and drizzle 
this afternoon primarily near and north of I-80. Taken 
altogether, the synoptic picture across the Great Lakes today is
quintessential of November.

This evening (especially after sunset), coverage of showers and
drizzle should increase across the area ahead of and 
immediately behind the cold front. Breezy northerly winds will 
follow the front and continue through the overnight hours thanks
to mixing forced by the initial bout of cold air advection and 
modest pressure rises (3hr rises of 3 to 4mb). Toward daybreak,
breaks in stratus may allow for temperatures to tumble with 
overnight lows favored to reach the mid 30s north of I-88 to 
around 40 elsewhere. 

As the sharp secondary upper-level wave races through the 
central Great Lakes throughout the day tomorrow, relatively warm
waters of Lake Huron and lingering baroclinicity along the 
frontal boundary will induce the development of a secondary 
center of low pressure somewhere near the thumb of Michigan. A 
relatively packed pressure gradient between the developing low 
and a building 1020mb high pressure system in the Upper 
Mississippi River Valley will establish a healthy pressure 
gradient centered on Lake Michigan leading to breezy northerly 
winds across our area. Associated robust low-level cold air 
advection will thus lead to a somewhat chilly day with highs 
poised to remain in the 40s to perhaps around 50. As the core of
the upper-level wave should pass largely toward Michigan, do 
anticipate a good deal of clearing in our local area (outside 
cyclonic shear axis). The exception will be in northwestern 
Indiana downstream of Lake Michigan where building 850mb to 
water temperature differentials will afford expansive stratus 
and lake effect rain showers. Based on the orientation of the 
wind field, currently anticipate a majority of lake effect 
showers to stream into LaPorte and Berrien counties just to the
northeast of our forecast area of responsibility. 

Friday night, the aforementioned surface high will build while 
moving southward through the Mississippi River Valley. Assuming 
stratus doesn't overstay its welcome, the combination of light 
winds, a dry airmass, and mostly clear skies should afford 
rapidly falling temperatures after sunset with overnight lows 
poised to reach the upper 20s to lower 30s away from Lake 
Michigan. 

The pattern turns rather banal this weekend onward as a cut- 
off low pressure system atop a surface high pressure system over
the southern US effectively forces a Rex Block across the 
central US. The eastward spread of Pacific air toward the Great 
Lakes will allow for daily temperatures to warm from this 
weekend into early next week with highs poised to return to the 
lower 60s by Monday. Ensemble guidance is hinting at a period of
cooler temperatures tied to amalgamation upper-level troughs 
over the eastern US by the end of next week, though am noting 
quite a bit of spread on the areal extent of any associated cold
pocket (850mb temperature spread reaches nearly 20C by Friday).
Will note a pitiful signal in ensemble guidance for meaningful 
rainfall locally anytime soon, consistent with CPC Day 6-10 and
8-14 day outlooks favoring below average precipitation in our 
area. Of course, this in tandem with above average temperatures 
also translates to no opportunities for snowflakes in our area
anytime soon.

Borchardt
